newsitem.title: USA: Centennial says probing results; fires chairman.
newsitem.headline: Centennial says probing results; fires chairman.

text.p: Centennial Technologies Inc., whose stock jumped more than fivefold last year, said Tuesday that it fired its chief executive officer and was checking the accuracy of its reported earnings for the latest quarter.

The Billerica, Mass-based maker of personal computer cards said it fired Chief Executive Officer Emanuel Pinez, relieved Chief Financial Officer James Murphy of his duties and notified the Securities and Exchange Commission of possible irregularities in its financial statements.

Just six weeks ago Centennial was the New York Stock Exchange's best performing issue of 1996. One week ago, it reported a 245 percent increase in 1996 sales to $51.2 million and net income of $5.9 million for the full year.
Now, trading in its stock is halted and it is uncertain when it will resume.

"We don't know when we're going to resume trading," Centennial's Treasurer Don Peck said in a telephone interview, adding that the firm's accountants, Coopers & Lybrand had been reviewing the books since early in the day.
He said Coopers & Lybrand's first job "is to review the situation and give us a time line."

Peck declined to specify what preliminary information prompted a special meeting of the company's board of directors Monday that lasted well into Tuesday morning, but what they found caused them to set up a special committee and conduct an inquiry. They are also starting a search for a new chief executive and an interim chief financial officer.
Pinez "is no longer with the company" Peck said, adding he was uncertain of the former chief's whereabouts.
In SEC filings, Pinez listed Beverly, Mass. as his home, but there was no telephone listing for him in that town some 45 minutes northeast of Boston, nor in any of the surrounding towns.
Centennial, which has about 18 million outstanding shares and as of Sept. 30 employed 117 people, has also hired as outside counsel the Boston law firm of Bingham Dana & Gould.
Meanwhile, the law firm of Milberg Weiss Bershad Hynes & Lerach filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of any shareholders who bought Centennial stock between Aug. 21, 1996 and Monday.
The civil complaint in Massachusetts federal court alleges that Centennial reported artificially inflated revenues and net earnings during that time.
Centennial's stock, closed Monday at $16.375 and never opened on Tuesday.
Last year, Centennial's stock jumped 451 percent, based on its closing price of $9.44 at year-end 1995 and $52 at the end of 1996.

The Billerica, Mass.-based firm said it was focusing on the earnings it reported for its fiscal second quarter ended Dec. 31 and financial statements for prior periods. The company reported net earnings of $3.46 million on sales of $31.7 million for the quarter vs. year-ago earnings of $996,269 on sales of $8.5 million.
The board has appointed a special committee comprised of four directors to oversee the inquiry, it said.

John Shields, vice-chairman of the board of directors, will chair the special committee. The special committee has engaged independent legal counsel to assist with the investigation, the company said, and independent auditors are assisting with this effort.
The special committee will also start a search for a CEO and an interim CFO. An article late last month in FinancialWorld questioned the company's accounting practices.
